description: redaction (ADR 0031, ADR 0020): what the seam withholds, said once for both tiers. The detector runs in the worker and the review of a finding is an Admin's action, so the two tiers have to agree about five things and only these five — which categories exist, what word stands in place of each, when a finding narrows the document, how the version string that rides on every finding is written, and what the always tier makes of a text a person types. This file is the contract and T-121's category descriptors derive it: name, tier, recogniser, threshold, context words, cues, placeholder and narrowing are one declaration per category in the worker, from which the analyzer registry and `rule_version` are built, and that table is held to this file. Nothing here names a part of a detector — no recogniser, no threshold, no model id — because the detector is T-121's and a fixture that named one would be the seam describing itself. The cases under `typed_text` keep to that: each is a text and the text it becomes, and says nothing of how. A category's `tier` is the tier it is ordinarily raised at, and one rule outranks it: the officer-block post-pass always wins, so a name inside an officers block is a `person-name` finding raised at the always tier and written into the row that way. **The placeholder follows the tier the finding was raised at, not the category**, which is why such a name is `[withheld]` with its block and not `[person A]`: the always set has one word for everything in it. The TypeScript half asserts against this tier's own boundary schemas (packages/core/test/sources/redaction.contract.test.ts); the Python half asserts against the columns the worker writes findings into (apps/worker/tests/redaction/test_redaction_contract.py). Neither holds the other's literals. The cases under `typed_text` are the one part both halves run alike: packages/core/test/llm/typed-text.test.ts through the api's own readers, and the Python half through the detector.

tiers.why: Policy: no connected source switches it off, so it carries no key on a connected source's rules in force. A span it withheld is restorable one at a time by an Admin with a reason, which is the only way it is ever let back into the text.
On unless a connected source says otherwise. The safe set an unconfigured connected source gets has this tier on, so a connected source nobody thought about withholds more rather than less.

Off unless a connected source says otherwise, because a bid library is full of the names and titles of people whose work the company is describing. Seeded on for meeting-note, support-ticket and HR-shaped connected sources, which is one flip of this key.

categories.why: An Article 9 kind — health first, and the condition the platform records is none until a health-sector client. Raised at sentence level, because a cue withheld out of its sentence leaves the sentence saying it anyway, and never inferred by a prompt.
A financial account identifier: the account number with its sort code. Policy because a company cannot consent on behalf of the person whose account it is.

An identifier the state issued to one person — in the United Kingdom the National Insurance number and the NHS number. Policy for the same reason, and one neutral word for all three of the always set, because a typed placeholder would tell the audience what class of data the document holds.
A date read as a person's, not a date. A bare date is never this category: a bid library is dates all the way down, and a seam that withheld them would return a document nobody could read.
Where a person lives, which in the United Kingdom is usually recognised from the postcode outward. The company's own registered office is an address and not this category.
A person's own email address or telephone number, as distinct from the company's published ones. Typed, because the reader has to know a way of reaching somebody was removed rather than a name.

A person's name, replaced by a stable pseudonym rather than a blank: the same name is the same letter everywhere in one connected source and a different letter in another, so a document still reads as a document and two connected sources cannot be joined on the letter. `[person A]` is the first letter, and the placeholder every later one is written in the shape of. This is the tier a name is ordinarily raised at; a name inside an officers block is raised at the always tier instead, whatever a connected source says, and takes that tier's word.
A person's role, which names them in a small company however the name is handled. Off by default because a bid is largely an account of who did what.

must_parse.why: the ordinary shape: the worker's own rule version, then a pin derived from the packages and the model id

the same string with a hashed pin — deliberately unlike the sample above, because the agreement pins the shape of the string and not the format of either part, and a tier that read a format into one would break on the first bump

must_not_parse.why: the rule version alone: a finding that named the rules and not the detector could not be re-baselined when the detector moved
two separators: the colon appears exactly once, so splitting on it is the same operation in both tiers whichever end they split from
a space where the separator goes
whitespace inside the string, which would make two versions that are the same version compare unequal

typed_text.why: Text a person types never passes the worker's seam, so the api reads it against the always tier with readers of its own. Each case is a text and what it becomes with the always tier alone in force. Both tiers run every case: the worker through its detector with both switchable tiers off, the api through its own readers. `expected` is what the worker's detector returned, so a case that surprises is the seam's own behaviour written down, and a change to it is a change both tiers make together. `categories` names the always-tier categories a case is about, whether or not it ends in a hit.

cases.name: a National Insurance number in a question
cases.input: Does the pension scheme need my National Insurance number AB 12 34 56 C before I join?
cases.expected: Does the pension scheme need my National Insurance number [withheld] before I join?
cases.why: The number goes and everything round it stays, the space before it too.

cases.name: a National Insurance number that opens the text
cases.input: AB123456C is on the starter form, is that enough for payroll?
cases.expected: [withheld] is on the starter form, is that enough for payroll?
cases.why: With no space before it, the number alone is taken.

cases.name: a National Insurance number in lower case
cases.input: Is ab123456c the number payroll holds for me?
cases.expected: Is [withheld] the number payroll holds for me?
cases.why: The pattern reads its letters in either case.

cases.name: a refused prefix after a space
cases.input: Is GB123456A a National Insurance number?
cases.expected: Is GB123456A a National Insurance number?
cases.why: GB is a prefix no National Insurance number takes, and a space before it changes nothing.

cases.name: a refused prefix that opens the text
cases.input: Gb123456A is the reference on the form, is that right?
cases.expected: Gb123456A is the reference on the form, is that right?
cases.why: The refusal holds where the text opens too, in either case of its letters.

cases.name: an NHS number
cases.input: Which form asks for an NHS number such as 999 000 0018?
cases.expected: Which form asks for an NHS number such as [withheld]?
cases.why: Ten digits that pass the NHS check digit, with or without their spaces.

cases.name: ten digits that fail the NHS check digit
cases.input: Is purchase order 4500012345 still open?
cases.expected: Is purchase order 4500012345 still open?
cases.why: An NHS number carries a check digit, and ten digits that fail it are left in the text.

cases.name: a sort code with its account number
cases.input: Can payroll pay expenses into sort code 20-00-00, account number 12345678?
cases.expected: Can payroll pay expenses into sort code [withheld]?
cases.why: One placeholder covers the sort code, the account number and what lies between them.

cases.name: two numbers nothing calls an account
cases.input: Is ticket 10-20-30 the same fault as ticket 12345678?
cases.expected: Is ticket 10-20-30 the same fault as ticket 12345678?
cases.why: Six digits and eight are a sort code and an account number only when a word before them or between them says so: account, sort, bank, payment or BACS.

cases.name: the word that names the pair sits between its numbers
cases.input: Can payroll pay expenses into 20-00-00, account number 12345678?
cases.expected: Can payroll pay expenses into [withheld]?
cases.why: A word between the two numbers names the pair as a word before them does.

cases.name: a word between the numbers that holds a naming word
cases.input: Ticket 10-20-30 was sorted under ref 12345678.
cases.expected: Ticket 10-20-30 was sorted under ref 12345678.
cases.why: Between the numbers only a naming word itself, or its plural, names the pair. Sorted is not sort.

cases.name: a colon joins the sort code to the word before it
cases.input: Ref:200000 account 12345678, is that the one on file?
cases.expected: Ref:[withheld], is that the one on file?
cases.why: The word between the numbers names the pair, and the colon that joins Ref to the sort code changes nothing.

cases.name: two pairs, one of them named
cases.input: Is 10-20-30 12345678 a ticket, or is sort code 20-00-00 account 87654321 the one we pay?
cases.expected: Is 10-20-30 12345678 a ticket, or is sort code [withheld] the one we pay?
cases.why: Each pair is read on its own: the word that names the second comes after the first, so the first stays in the text.

cases.name: a sort code and account number on two lines
cases.input:
Sort code 20-00-00
account 12345678
Is that the account expenses go to?
cases.expected:
Sort code [withheld]
Is that the account expenses go to?
cases.why: What lies between the two numbers may hold a line break.

cases.name: two numbers too far apart to be a pair
cases.input: Is sort code 20-00-00 the one we gave the auditors last year, and is 12345678 the old account?
cases.expected: Is sort code 20-00-00 the one we gave the auditors last year, and is 12345678 the old account?
cases.why: An account number more than forty characters after the sort code is not read with it.

cases.name: the word that names the pair is joined to its sort code
cases.input: Do expenses go to 200000.account 12345678?
cases.expected: Do expenses go to [withheld]?
cases.why: A word between the numbers names the pair even when nothing parts it from the sort code.

cases.name: a one-sentence question that holds a cue
cases.input: Do you have a sickness absence policy?
cases.expected: [withheld]
cases.why: A special-category cue withholds its whole sentence, so a one-sentence question reaches the model as the placeholder alone.

cases.name: a cue in one sentence of three
cases.input: Who signs off a return to work? I was diagnosed with asthma last month. What does the handbook say?
cases.expected: Who signs off a return to work? [withheld] What does the handbook say?
cases.why: Only the cue's sentence goes, and the cue is read in any of its forms: diagnosed is a form of diagnose.

cases.name: a misspelt cue the worker reads by its ending
cases.input: My manager keeps diagnoseing me with anxiety, who do I tell?
cases.expected: [withheld]
cases.why: The worker finds a cue by taking an ending off the written word, so it reads diagnoseing as diagnose. A list of a cue's correct forms does not hold it.

cases.name: a misspelt plural of a cue
cases.input: How many diagnosises did the clinic record last year?
cases.expected: [withheld]
cases.why: The same for a noun: the worker reads diagnosises as more than one diagnosis.

cases.name: space round a cue's sentence
cases.input: Which staff are on medication this week
cases.expected: [withheld]
cases.why: The space before a sentence and after it is no part of it, so it stays.

cases.name: a blank line ends a sentence
cases.input:
Who is on medication this week

Where is the rota kept
cases.expected:
[withheld]

Where is the rota kept
cases.why: Lines typed with no full stop are still two sentences when a blank line parts them.

cases.name: words near a cue that are not one
cases.input: Who approves sick leave, and where is the diagnostic report for the boiler?
cases.expected: Who approves sick leave, and where is the diagnostic report for the boiler?
cases.why: Sick and diagnostic are not forms of sickness, diagnose or diagnosis.

cases.name: a cue set off by underscores
cases.input: Was she _diagnosed_ before her start date?
cases.expected: [withheld]
cases.why: The worker's tokenizer takes an underscore off either end of a word, so the cue is read. To a pattern's \b an underscore is one more letter of the word.

cases.name: a question with nothing to withhold
cases.input: How long is the notice period for a framework contract?
cases.expected: How long is the notice period for a framework contract?
cases.why: It comes back byte for byte.

cases.name: a person's name
cases.input: Does Rosalind Petheridge still lead the audit team?
cases.expected: Does Rosalind Petheridge still lead the audit team?
cases.why: The stated limit. The always tier holds no names outside an officers block, and a name needs the detector's model, which the api tier cannot run.

cases.name: two hits in one question
cases.input: Is NHS number 999 000 0018 hers, and is sort code 20-00-00 account 12345678 the one on file?
cases.expected: Is NHS number [withheld] hers, and is sort code [withheld] the one on file?
cases.why: Each hit takes its own placeholder, and the text between them stays as typed.

cases.name: an identifier inside a cue's sentence
cases.input: She was diagnosed last year, and her NHS number is 999 000 0018. Who holds the record?
cases.expected: [withheld] Who holds the record?
cases.why: A hit inside a longer one is written under the longer one's placeholder, so the sentence takes one placeholder and not two.

cases.name: a pair that runs into a cue's sentence
cases.input: Sort code 20-00-00. Was account 12345678 opened after her diagnosis?
cases.expected: Sort code [withheld][withheld]
cases.why: The pair crosses the full stop into the cue's sentence. The longer hit keeps its span and the other keeps the characters left over, under a placeholder of its own.

cases.name: a pair that runs out of a cue's sentence
cases.input: Is her diagnosis why sort code 20-00-00 changed? The account is 12345678.
cases.expected: [withheld][withheld].
cases.why: The same the other way round: the pair starts in the cue's sentence and keeps what follows it, the space after the question mark included.

cases.name: a next-line character ends a sentence
cases.input: Sickness absence rose.Who reports it?
cases.expected: [withheld]Who reports it?
cases.why: Python's whitespace holds U+0085 and JavaScript's \s does not.

cases.name: a byte-order mark does not end a sentence
cases.input: Sickness absence rose.﻿ Who reports it?
cases.expected: [withheld]
cases.why: JavaScript's \s holds U+FEFF and Python's whitespace does not, so the worker reads one sentence here.

cases.name: a letter outside ASCII joins a National Insurance number
cases.input: Is caféAB123456C a National Insurance number?
cases.expected: Is caféAB123456C a National Insurance number?
cases.why: The number must stand apart from the letters round it, and the worker counts é as a letter. JavaScript's \b does not.

cases.name: a letter outside ASCII joins an account number
cases.input: Is sort code 20-00-00 account 12345678é ours?
cases.expected: Is sort code 20-00-00 account 12345678é ours?
cases.why: The same boundary, read by the worker's other regex engine.

cases.name: digits outside ASCII in a sort code and account number
cases.input: Is sort code ٢٠-٠٠-٠٠ account ١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨ ours?
cases.expected: Is sort code [withheld] ours?
cases.why: Python's \d reads any decimal digit and JavaScript's reads 0 to 9.
